narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this probability exceeded their threshold, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school—far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 38 worked in the opposite direction. It sits slightly above the average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction modestly toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class standings.

The remaining details—your 3.4 undergraduate GPA (above the accepted average), middle family income, full-time study plans, gender, and race—played only minor roles. The model ignored gender and race entirely when making its forecast.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Raising your class rank in future years or boosting your LSAT score would most effectively lower your predicted risk of failure. Consider retaking the LSAT or seeking targeted academic support before reapplying.
